title: Microsoft's Brad Smith says AI needs global rules: less oversight than milk
excerpt: In a BBC interview, Microsoft's president urged mandatory emergency brakes, incident reports and independent evaluation of AI systems — and said Britain's AI Security Institute is best placed to lead.
body:
• Microsoft president Brad Smith told the BBC that AI faces fewer safety rules than milk or washing machines, and urged a global regulatory framework with real enforcement.
  • His proposals: mandatory "emergency brakes" on AI systems, legal incident reports, a duty to inform victims of rogue-agent breaches, and independent evaluators vetting new models.
  • Smith says Britain's AI Security Institute is best placed to lead global standard-setting, contrasting Washington's self-regulation stance with Brussels' risk-based AI Act.
  • No new law has been enacted — these are proposals, and the White House currently favors voluntary industry commitments.

Microsoft president Brad Smith has called for global safety rules for artificial intelligence with real legal force, arguing that the world's most powerful technology currently faces less regulatory scrutiny than a carton of milk. Speaking in an interview with the BBC, reported by Reuters on October 12, 2026, Smith said it was time to apply the product-safety playbook used for everything from appliances to food to AI systems.

Context & Background

Smith's central comparison was deliberately homely: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection," he told the BBC's Big Boss Interview, published October 11. "We know how to do this for other products. We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

"Context & Background Smith's central comparison was deliberately homely: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI."

The remarks land in the middle of a widening global debate over agentic AI — systems that can take actions, not just produce text. Anthropic and OpenAI have recently begun disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents, and researchers have warned of escalating risks as capabilities advance. At the same time, some in the industry have called for slowing development, a demand that has drawn suspicion that incumbent firms are trying to set rules that preserve their own lead.

"Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

— Brad Smith, President of Microsoft, to the BBC

Impact & Analysis

Smith's proposals are more concrete than the voluntary commitments that have dominated AI governance so far. He wants a global set of safety rules that would require companies to build "emergency brakes" into AI systems, to write formal incident reports when things go wrong, and to inform and take responsibility toward a "victim" if a rogue AI agent breaches their systems. New developments would be vetted by independent evaluators before release.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=jFM4nb3lUHI

That goes further than the industry accord signed at President Donald Trump's "Super Intelligence" summit, where executives from Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and others agreed to voluntary safeguards and independent audits. Smith said he was "happy to sign it" but that voluntary promises were "not sufficient any longer," arguing the concern is the less responsible companies that will not police themselves.

He also drew a sharp geographic contrast. Officials in Washington view London very differently from Brussels, he said: the EU regulates AI by risk tier under its AI Act, while the Trump administration favors self-regulation so US firms do not lose ground to China. For Smith, the country best placed to lead is Britain, thanks to its AI Security Institute — launched under former prime minister Rishi Sunak and given pre-deployment access to frontier models under voluntary agreements with the major labs.

Diaspora Angle

For the millions of Indian engineers, researchers and founders working across the AI supply chain — from Bengaluru's labs to Seattle's campuses — the regulatory patchwork is already a daily cost: products must satisfy the EU's AI Act, navigate Washington's hands-off posture, and now watch for a possible UK-led standard. Engineers shipping AI agents can follow Smith's full proposals in the Reuters report on the BBC interview and track how the UK's AI Security Institute, currently engaging frontier-model developers, turns voluntary access into binding rules.

What's Next

Nothing is law yet. The UK's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, was preparing to urge frontier-model developers to do more on risk and safeguards as Smith's interview went out, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has separately argued AI systems must be observable, testable and containable. The open question is whether any government converts proposals like Smith's into obligations — or whether voluntary accords remain the ceiling while the technology keeps accelerating.
